firstSteps: Pick five to ten pieces of hardware and confirm each mission's facts in the NSSDCA catalog.
Pull an LROC featured-site image (or a HiRISE image for Mars) showing each piece where it sits today.
Search the NASA Image Library for launch and on-surface photos to pair with each orbital view.
abandoned-but-not-forgotten.note: Official resource lists open on the Space Apps site on Nov 13; the Moon side is far better covered by public imagery than deep space.

firstSteps: Pick a variable the statement names (MERRA-2, GLDAS, AIRS, GPM or MODIS) and preview it for one region in Giovanni.
Download a daily or monthly series for that region, long enough for a statistical test.
Test the trend with Mann-Kendall or a t-test and report the rate of change per year.
earth-system-trend-detective.note: Giovanni and the gridded files need a free Earthdata Login; register before the hackathon starts.

firstSteps: Pick two or three core resources, such as life support, power and shielding, and write the rules that link them.
Use DONKI solar events and RAD dose readings as real inputs for radiation risk.
Show players which NASA data drives each event, and label embedded data as archived, not live.
junior-astronaut-mission-trainer.note: No NASA dataset gives life-support numbers directly; cite NTRS reports for any figures you use.

firstSteps: Run the Horizons starter to get Sun and Earth elevation for one south pole site.
Overlay the Moon Trek illumination and Earth visibility layers to shortlist candidate sites.
Pull LOLA topography for your sites, since local terrain can block a low Sun or Earth.
clps-lunar-mission-browser.note: Horizons gives elevation over a smooth horizon; terrain shadowing needs LOLA elevation data.

firstSteps: Search OSDR for bone, heart and radiation studies to learn which indicators researchers measure.
Use DONKI particle events to simulate when a crew's radiation risk rises.
Define your health indicators and alert thresholds, citing the NTRS or OSDR sources you used.
astronaut-health-monitoring.note: Individual astronaut health records are privacy-protected; plan on simulated crew data built from published ranges.

firstSteps: Create an Earthdata Login and run the NISAR GCOV starter for your area of interest.
Preview coverage in the GIBS NISAR layer or ASF Search before downloading any large HDF5 files.
Pick one change story (flooding, burn scar, crop cycle, ground motion) and gather before and after scenes.
dancing-with-the-sars.note: NISAR products in CMR are labeled provisional or beta; Sentinel-1 OPERA RTC is the validated fallback.

firstSteps: Run the POWER starter for your farm's coordinates to get rainfall, temperature and sunlight.
Add SMAP soil moisture, ECOSTRESS heat stress and GPM rainfall, resampled to one common grid.
Compare at least three rotations, including the current one, with the evidence and risks for each.
field-shift-adapting-farms.note: Local soil and crop data are not NASA products; plan on sourcing them from a partner or a public soil survey.

firstSteps: Browse PSI's combustion investigations (BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME) and note which include raw data.
Run the NTRS starter to collect the papers behind those investigations.
Choose the attributes your dashboard compares (fuel, oxygen level, airflow, sensors) and test summaries on five investigations by hand.
flame-in-freefall.note: Coverage is thin: PSI has no documented public API, so expect manual downloads. Official resource lists open on the Space Apps site on Nov 13.

firstSteps: Request a free FIRMS MAP_KEY and pull MODIS_SP and VIIRS_SNPP_SP detections for one test area.
Compare detection counts in the 2012 onward overlap years to see how the two sensors differ.
Sketch the burning-activity calendar using GIBS fire layers before building the full pipeline.
Pick a target base site on the Moon or Mars and describe its terrain, lighting and surface from Trek layers.
Turn that description into measurable Earth criteria (slope, elevation, vegetation, temperature).
Screen candidate Earth regions using SRTM elevation and HLS imagery.
Load the Mars Trek CTX mosaic and MOLA hillshade layers into a web map.
Pick a route and pull HiRISE images and terrain models along it.
Mark hazards (slopes, boulders) and science targets, then add at least one more data type, such as thermal or radiation.
martian-map.note: Official resource lists open on the Space Apps site on Nov 13; THEMIS day and night thermal-infrared mosaics are also in Mars Trek.

firstSteps: Run the SPHEREx starter to list repeat visits of the sky around WISE 0855 (RA 08h55m10.8s, Dec -7d14m42.5s).
Blink those visits in time order and check the brown dwarf moves against its AllWISE position.
Repeat for the statement's other test targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.
planet-x-and-spherex.note: SPHEREx data are Quick Release products and will change; check the IRSA SPHEREx page for the latest release.

firstSteps: Define the trade-offs your game scores (mass, power, budget, data return) and keep the first version small.
Use SBDB and Horizons so targets and travel distances come from real orbits.
Pull spacecraft models from NASA 3D Resources and images from the NASA Image Library for the UI.
space-mission-design-game.note: Real costs and masses are scattered across mission reports; cite the NTRS sources you use.

firstSteps: Browse Earth.gov and the SVS to pick two or three visualizations with a clear story.
Find a numeric series behind each one (GISTEMP, POWER, or GIBS layers) to drive the sound.
Map one variable to pitch or tempo and test it with someone who has not seen the visuals.
